publicationLaw: One improving canonical URL per useful topic. Every page must add source-grounded understanding or product utility, keep source and interpretation separate, and reuse existing 4PLANET / NATUREBRAIN / ATLAS infrastructure.

earthNow.title: Earth Now — What Is Happening on Earth Right Now? | 4PLANET
earthNow.description: Explore the latest available source-grounded signals across Earth — fires, earthquakes, natural events, coral heat stress, forest change, atmosphere and biodiversity — through 4PLANET ATLAS.
earthNow.answer: Earth Now is a public 4PLANET window into the latest available planetary signals from authoritative sources. Different datasets update at different speeds, so every layer keeps its own source and time semantics instead of being labelled generically as live.

signals.label: Wildfires + thermal anomalies
signals.detail: Satellite-detected heat and source-reported fire events.

signals.label: Earthquakes
signals.detail: Recent recorded seismic events from the USGS global feed.

signals.label: Fire event reports
signals.detail: Source-reported wildfire and fire events from NASA EONET.

signals.label: Coral heat stress
signals.detail: Satellite-derived accumulated thermal stress on reefs.

signals.label: Forest change
signals.detail: Mapped tree-cover-loss context with separate forest assessment evidence.

signals.label: Aerosol and air-quality context
signals.detail: Satellite aerosol context alongside air-quality evidence; not a ground-level reading.

signals.label: Climate-related ocean conditions
signals.detail: Sea-surface temperature context used alongside broader climate evidence.

signals.label: Life observations
signals.detail: Open biodiversity records and occurrence density with sampling limitations.

earthNow.truthBoundary: Earth Now means latest available from each source, not one synchronized real-time Earth. Historical records, delayed composites and source failures remain labelled according to their own meaning.

topics.name: Wildfires
topics.title: Wildfires — Global Fire Signals, Maps and Sources | 4PLANET
topics.description: Explore satellite thermal anomalies and source-reported wildfire events with 4PLANET ATLAS, including source dates and clear limits on what the data proves.
topics.answer: Wildfire monitoring combines several kinds of evidence. Satellite thermal anomalies can reveal unusual heat, while event feeds report incidents under their own definitions. Neither should be treated as proof of local conditions without checking the source, time and context.
keyFacts: Thermal anomalies detect heat, not cause.
NASA event records and satellite layers have different update rules.
4PLANET keeps signal, event and interpretation separate.
topics.happening: The embedded ATLAS view exposes the latest available fire and natural-event layers configured in 4PLANET. Read each source date before treating a record as current.
topics.whyItMatters: Fire information changes quickly. A stable, source-aware page makes it possible to inspect the map without turning every heat pixel into a wildfire claim.
topics.sourceEstablishes: NASA satellite products can establish detected thermal anomalies for defined observation periods, while EONET can establish events carried by its source feed.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: A thermal anomaly alone does not establish a wildfire, its cause, local danger or ecological outcome.
topics.atlasContextNote: The fire layer contains satellite-detected heat. It is not a local emergency service.

sources.label: Fire Information for Resource Management System
Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker v3

topics.name: Earthquakes
topics.title: Earthquakes Today — Global Map and USGS Data | 4PLANET
topics.description: Explore recent earthquakes worldwide through 4PLANET ATLAS using USGS source records, with magnitude, time, place and clear interpretation limits.
topics.answer: Earthquakes are sudden releases of energy in the Earth’s crust. 4PLANET uses the USGS global feed to place recent recorded events on the same ATLAS used for other planetary signals.
keyFacts: The ATLAS earthquake layer uses the USGS global feed.
Magnitude, time, place and depth belong to the source record.
An earthquake record does not automatically establish ecological impact.
topics.happening: The embedded map reads the recent USGS earthquake layer available in ATLAS. Freshness belongs to the source feed and individual event timestamps.
topics.whyItMatters: Earthquake searches spike during major events. A permanent page can remain useful between events while directing people to the original records.
topics.sourceEstablishes: USGS source records can establish reported event location, time, magnitude, depth and event metadata.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: The event record alone does not establish local damage, ecological consequence or safety conditions.
topics.atlasContextNote: Use official civil-protection sources for local safety decisions.

topics.name: Climate Change
topics.title: Climate Change — Evidence, Signals and Solutions | 4PLANET
topics.description: Understand climate change through source-grounded evidence, planetary signals and connected solutions, with IPCC sources and 4PLANET ATLAS context.
topics.answer: Climate change is a long-term shift in the climate system. The IPCC’s latest completed assessment is AR6; 4PLANET connects that evidence to observable planetary layers without pretending one map layer represents the whole climate system.
keyFacts: Climate is a long-term system, not a single weather event.
Different observations have different time scales and uncertainties.
Mitigation, adaptation and ecological response are separate but connected questions.
topics.happening: ATLAS can place temperature-related, sea-ice, vegetation, aerosol and other source layers beside one another. They should be read according to each source’s own date and method.
topics.whyItMatters: Climate change touches ecosystems, infrastructure, food, health and economies. Clear source boundaries matter because individual signals are often overinterpreted.
topics.sourceEstablishes: IPCC assessments synthesize the state of scientific knowledge across physical science, impacts, adaptation and mitigation.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: A single local event or one ATLAS layer cannot by itself establish attribution to climate change.
topics.atlasContextNote: The layers have different temporal coverage and should not be read as one combined climate score.

topics.name: Biodiversity
topics.title: Biodiversity — Species Records, Patterns and Sources | 4PLANET
topics.description: Explore biodiversity through open species occurrence data, source-grounded explanations and 4PLANET ATLAS without confusing records with abundance.
topics.answer: Biodiversity describes the variety of life at genetic, species and ecosystem levels. 4PLANET uses open biodiversity records as evidence of reported occurrences, not as a complete census of life.
keyFacts: Occurrence records show where a source reported an organism.
More records can reflect more observation effort, not more life.
Species, places and living systems need distinct evidence layers.
topics.happening: The ATLAS biodiversity view shows GBIF record density and selected occurrence layers. Bright or dense areas can indicate recording intensity rather than ecological abundance.
topics.whyItMatters: Biodiversity data becomes misleading when observation effort is confused with biological reality. The page keeps that limitation visible.
topics.sourceEstablishes: GBIF provides open access to occurrence records and taxonomic data supplied by its publishing network.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: Record density alone does not establish abundance, complete range, population trend or ecosystem health.
topics.atlasContextNote: Record density is partly a map of where people have looked.

sources.label: Global Assessment of Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

topics.name: Deforestation
topics.title: Deforestation and Forest Change — Maps, Data and Context | 4PLANET
topics.description: Explore forest change through authoritative assessments and mapped tree-cover loss, with clear distinctions between tree-cover loss and deforestation.
topics.answer: Deforestation is the conversion of forest to another land use. Tree-cover loss is a different measure: it can include harvest, fire, storms and other temporary or permanent changes.
keyFacts: Tree-cover loss is not automatically deforestation.
National forest assessments and satellite products answer different questions.
Time, threshold and land-use definitions must remain visible.
topics.happening: ATLAS exposes a Global Forest Watch / UMD tree-cover-loss layer as spatial context. FAO’s FRA 2025 provides the latest global official national-data assessment.
topics.whyItMatters: Forest change is central to climate, biodiversity and livelihoods, but different datasets use different definitions. Conflating them produces false conclusions.
topics.sourceEstablishes: FAO FRA 2025 reports official national forest-resource trends; mapped tree-cover-loss products show detected canopy-loss patterns under their own methods.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: A tree-cover-loss pixel by itself does not establish deforestation, illegality, cause or permanence.
topics.atlasContextNote: The map layer is tree-cover loss, not a direct deforestation verdict.

topics.name: Plastic Pollution
topics.title: Plastic Pollution — Evidence, Systems and Solutions | 4PLANET
topics.description: Understand plastic pollution across production, use, waste and environmental leakage, with UNEP sources and ocean-system context.
topics.answer: Plastic pollution is a system problem spanning material production, product design, consumption, waste management and leakage into land and water. No single ocean map measures the whole problem.
keyFacts: Plastic pollution begins before litter reaches the ocean.
Different polymers, products and chemicals create different risks.
Prevention, reuse, collection and treatment solve different parts of the system.
topics.happening: 4PLANET currently uses ATLAS here as environmental context, not as a global plastic-pollution measurement layer.
topics.whyItMatters: Plastic is useful but persistent waste and leakage can create long-lived environmental pressures. The solution space is wider than clean-up alone.
topics.sourceEstablishes: UNEP documents plastic pollution as a global environmental challenge and tracks the international process for a legally binding instrument.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: The ATLAS context view does not establish local plastic concentration, clean-up performance or ecological outcome.
topics.atlasContextNote: This is contextual geography, not a plastic-concentration layer.

sources.label: Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee on Plastic Pollution

topics.name: Coral Bleaching
topics.title: Coral Bleaching — Heat Stress, Reef Context and Sources | 4PLANET
topics.description: Explore coral heat stress and bleaching context using NOAA Coral Reef Watch layers, with a clear boundary between heat stress and observed bleaching.
topics.answer: Coral bleaching can occur when corals experience stress, especially prolonged heat. NOAA Degree Heating Weeks measure accumulated thermal stress; they are a pressure indicator, not direct observation of bleaching on every reef.
keyFacts: Degree Heating Weeks accumulate heat stress over time.
Heat stress and observed bleaching are different evidence types.
Local reef condition still requires field evidence.
topics.happening: The ATLAS coral layer uses NOAA Coral Reef Watch heat-stress data where available.
topics.whyItMatters: Heat-stress maps are powerful early-warning context, but overclaiming them as direct reef condition hides what still needs field observation.
topics.sourceEstablishes: NOAA Coral Reef Watch products establish satellite-derived thermal-stress conditions under defined methods and spatial resolution.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: Heat stress alone does not establish that every coral in a mapped area has bleached or died.
topics.atlasLabel: Coral heat stress and sea-surface temperature
topics.atlasContextNote: Heat stress is pressure evidence, not a direct bleaching census.

sources.label: Daily 5 km Coral Bleaching Heat Stress Monitoring

topics.name: Air Quality
topics.title: Air Quality — Pollution, Aerosols and What the Data Means | 4PLANET
topics.description: Understand air quality through WHO health context and satellite aerosol data, while keeping aerosol optical depth separate from ground-level pollution measurements.
topics.answer: Air quality describes the concentration of pollutants people and ecosystems are exposed to. Satellite aerosol optical depth can show particles in the atmospheric column, but it is not the same as a ground-level air-quality measurement.
keyFacts: Air pollution is a major environmental health risk.
Satellite aerosol data and surface monitors measure different things.
Local exposure requires appropriate ground-level measurements and methods.
topics.happening: ATLAS exposes a NASA aerosol optical-depth layer as planetary context. It should be read as a proxy, not as a local PM2.5 reading.
topics.whyItMatters: People often interpret colourful atmospheric maps as direct exposure. Keeping measurement type explicit prevents that error.
topics.sourceEstablishes: WHO provides health evidence and guideline context; NASA satellite products provide atmospheric observations under their own retrieval methods.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: ATLAS aerosol optical depth does not by itself establish the pollution concentration a person is breathing at ground level.
topics.atlasContextNote: Aerosol optical depth is an atmospheric-column measure, not a ground monitor.

topics.name: Orca
topics.title: Orca — Species, Observations and Ocean Context | 4PLANET
topics.description: Meet the orca through source-grounded species intelligence and reported occurrence records, connected to 4PLANET ATLAS and WH4LES_.
topics.answer: Orca, Orcinus orca, is a globally distributed toothed whale with distinct populations and ecotypes. 4PLANET keeps species-level facts, population-level evidence and individual occurrence records separate.
keyFacts: An occurrence point is not a live animal position.
Different orca populations can have different status and pressures.
Species identity stays connected across SPECIES and ATLAS.
topics.happening: The embedded ATLAS view shows reported cetacean occurrence context. It is not an orca tracker.
topics.whyItMatters: Orca is an ideal example of why species intelligence needs identity, place, population and source boundaries rather than a single generic profile.
topics.sourceEstablishes: NOAA and biodiversity data sources can establish population-specific status information and source-reported occurrence records.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: A set of occurrence points does not establish a migration route, current position or population abundance.
topics.atlasContextNote: Reported observations are historical/source records, not a live tracker.

topics.name: Whales
topics.title: Whales — Species, Occurrence Records and Ocean Context | 4PLANET
topics.description: Explore whale and dolphin occurrence records, species connections and ocean context without confusing observations with live tracks or population size.
topics.answer: Whales are diverse marine mammals recorded across many scientific and observation datasets. 4PLANET treats each record as evidence with its own place, time and source rather than turning points into a live migration map.
keyFacts: OBIS and GBIF aggregate occurrence records from many datasets.
Record count is not population size.
Observation points do not automatically form a migration route.
topics.happening: ATLAS exposes a bounded cetacean occurrence layer and connects relevant records into species journeys.
topics.whyItMatters: Marine observations are sparse and uneven. Honest interpretation makes the data useful without making it look more complete than it is.
topics.sourceEstablishes: OBIS and GBIF records can establish that contributing sources reported occurrences with available time and location metadata.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: The records alone do not establish current occupancy, abundance or complete distribution.
topics.atlasContextNote: The current ATLAS whale layer is bounded and incomplete by design.

topics.name: Bees
topics.title: Bees and Pollinators — Biodiversity, Pollination and Sources | 4PLANET
topics.description: Understand bees and pollinators through IPBES evidence and biodiversity records, connected to 4PLANET species and land-system context.
topics.answer: Bees are a diverse group of pollinators, and pollination connects wild plants, crops and ecosystem processes. Pressures and responses differ across species and places.
keyFacts: Pollination is an ecosystem service involving many animal groups.
Not all bee species have the same ecology or trend.
Occurrence records show observations, not total population.
topics.happening: ATLAS provides broader biodiversity and occurrence context; it is not a complete bee abundance map.
topics.whyItMatters: Pollinators connect biodiversity and food systems, but generic claims about ‘the bees’ can hide major differences between species and regions.
topics.sourceEstablishes: IPBES assesses pollinator status, drivers, ecosystem-service relationships and policy responses; GBIF provides source occurrence records.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: A mapped occurrence or global assessment does not determine the status of every local bee population.
topics.atlasContextNote: The map is broader biodiversity context, not a bee-population census.

sources.label: Assessment Report on Pollinators, Pollination and Food Production

topics.name: Amazon Rainforest
topics.title: Amazon Rainforest — Forest Change, Fire and Biodiversity | 4PLANET
topics.description: Explore Amazonia through forest-change, fire and biodiversity context with source-grounded maps and clear boundaries between observations and interpretation.
topics.answer: The Amazon is a continental forest system spanning multiple countries, ecosystems and human communities. No single polygon or dataset fully represents it.
keyFacts: Land-cover maps, fire detections and biodiversity records measure different things.
Amazonia crosses national and ecological boundaries.
Fire detection does not by itself establish deforestation.
topics.happening: The ATLAS view combines global fire, forest-change and biodiversity layers focused on Amazonia without creating a separate Amazon-only data system.
topics.whyItMatters: The Amazon links biodiversity, water, climate and human systems at enormous scale. Source definitions and boundaries determine what conclusions are valid.
topics.sourceEstablishes: MapBiomas Amazonia provides annual land-cover mapping under explicit methods; NASA fire systems provide time-bounded thermal observations.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: These layers alone do not establish cause, illegality, land tenure or ecological outcome for a specific change.
topics.atlasLabel: Amazonia forest, fire and biodiversity context
topics.atlasContextNote: Multiple sources are shown together but retain separate meanings.

sources.label: Fire Information for Resource Management System

topics.name: Oslofjord
topics.title: Oslofjord — State, Pressures, Evidence and Map | 4PLANET
topics.description: Explore Oslofjord through source-grounded place intelligence, environmental status and mapped context, including the bounded Bunnefjorden proof case.
topics.answer: Oslofjord is a complex coastal system affected by several pressures. 4PLANET keeps whole-fjord status separate from the narrower Bunnefjorden case where specific oxygen conditions and an infrastructure intervention can be inspected.
keyFacts: Whole-fjord state and Bunnefjorden evidence are different scopes.
Water status, habitat interventions and bathymetry come from different source systems.
A measured oxygen improvement is not proof that the whole fjord is restored.
topics.happening: The embedded ATLAS offers ocean and biodiversity context. The deeper Living Systems page carries the bounded Bunnefjorden evidence case.
topics.whyItMatters: Oslofjord is close enough to be personally legible and complex enough to demonstrate how place, pressure, actors and evidence should be connected.
topics.sourceEstablishes: Miljødirektoratet reports on wider fjord condition; NIVA provides bounded evidence on Bunnefjorden oxygen and deep-water renewal.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: A local intervention result cannot be generalized into recovery of the entire Oslofjord ecosystem.
topics.atlasContextNote: Use the Living Systems page for the bounded Bunnefjorden evidence chain.

sources.label: Mulighetsvurdering – Overføring av Gjersjøvann til Bunnefjorden

topics.name: Renewable Energy
topics.title: Renewable Energy — Data, Technologies and System Context | 4PLANET
topics.description: Understand renewable energy through IRENA and IEA data, connected to energy-system and emissions context without reducing trade-offs to a single score.
topics.answer: Renewable energy comes from sources replenished on human timescales, including solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal and bioenergy. Deployment, grids, materials, land and reliability remain part of the system question.
keyFacts: Renewable technologies have different resource and system profiles.
Installed capacity is not the same as electricity generated.
Grid, storage, permitting and supply chains affect deployment.
topics.happening: IRENA’s 2026 statistics cover renewable capacity through 2025; IEA’s latest renewable analysis provides deployment and system context.
topics.whyItMatters: Energy underpins almost every human system. Comparing technologies requires more than a simple green/not-green label.
topics.sourceEstablishes: IRENA and IEA provide capacity, technology and market/system data using documented methods.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: A global capacity trend does not determine the best technology, site or grid choice for a specific project.
topics.atlasContextNote: Night lights and emissions are context layers, not a renewable-capacity map.

topics.name: Solar Energy
topics.title: Solar Energy — Solar PV Data, Growth and System Context | 4PLANET
topics.description: Understand solar PV through IEA and IRENA data, including capacity, generation and system context with clear limits on what global statistics imply locally.
topics.answer: Solar photovoltaics convert sunlight directly into electricity. Their value depends not only on panel performance but on location, grid conditions, storage, demand, finance, materials and land or rooftop use.
keyFacts: Capacity and generation are different measures.
Solar output varies by location and time.
Grid integration and storage can matter as deployment scales.
topics.happening: IEA’s solar page carries current technology tracking; IRENA publishes comparable global capacity statistics.
topics.whyItMatters: Solar is expanding rapidly, but useful decisions need local resource, system and economic context rather than global averages alone.
topics.sourceEstablishes: IEA and IRENA provide historical and current technology/capacity data under documented definitions.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: Global deployment data does not establish the economics or environmental performance of a specific installation.
topics.atlasContextNote: The current map is contextual; 4PLANET does not yet expose a global solar-capacity layer here.

topics.name: Food Waste
topics.title: Food Waste — Scale, Measurement and Solutions | 4PLANET
topics.description: Understand food waste across households, food service and retail using UNEP evidence, linked to the wider food system and practical reduction pathways.
topics.answer: Food waste is edible or associated food material discarded across households, food service and retail. Measurement matters because prevention strategies depend on where and why waste occurs.
keyFacts: Food waste is measured across different sectors.
Comparable measurement is essential for tracking reduction.
Prevention and redistribution are different from downstream waste treatment.
topics.happening: UNEP’s Food Waste Index Report 2024 is the core current global reference used on this page.
topics.whyItMatters: Wasted food also embodies land, water, energy, labour and money. Reducing it can improve both household and system efficiency.
topics.sourceEstablishes: UNEP provides global estimates, sector measurement guidance and documented approaches to reducing food waste.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: Global estimates do not determine the waste level of a specific household, business or city without local measurement.
topics.atlasContextNote: The map is context for human systems; it is not a food-waste measurement layer.

topics.name: Fast Fashion
topics.title: Fast Fashion — Materials, Impacts and Circular Solutions | 4PLANET
topics.description: Understand fast fashion as a textile value-chain problem involving materials, chemicals, labour, overproduction, consumption and waste.
topics.answer: Fast fashion is a business and consumption model built around rapid product turnover and high volumes. Its environmental effects span fibres, chemicals, energy, water, production, transport, use and end-of-life.
keyFacts: Textile impacts occur across the full value chain.
Durability, repair, reuse and circularity address different stages.
Company claims need source-specific verification.
topics.happening: UNEP’s textile work provides the evidence and policy context; 4PLANET connects the topic to F4SHION_ and future company intelligence.
topics.whyItMatters: Fashion is both a material system and a cultural system. That makes product design, business models and consumer behaviour relevant together.
topics.sourceEstablishes: UNEP documents environmental risks across the textile lifecycle and work toward sustainable and circular textile systems.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: Sector-level evidence does not prove the environmental performance of an individual brand or garment.
topics.atlasContextNote: The map is system context, not a fashion supply-chain trace.

sources.label: Environmental permitting in the textile value chain

topics.name: Rewilding
topics.title: Rewilding — Principles, Evidence and Restoration Context | 4PLANET
topics.description: Understand rewilding through IUCN guidance, ecological-process recovery and place-based evidence rather than a single universal intervention.
topics.answer: Rewilding aims to restore ecological integrity by enabling natural processes, relationships and dynamic ecosystems to recover. It is not one fixed technique and requires place-specific goals, people, monitoring and adaptation.
keyFacts: Rewilding focuses on ecological processes and integrity.
Local engagement and monitoring matter.
Interventions and acceptable outcomes differ by place.
topics.happening: IUCN published new rewilding guidelines in 2025; 4PLANET connects those principles to place, species and restoration context.
topics.whyItMatters: Rewilding is increasingly used as a broad label. Clear principles help separate genuine ecological recovery work from vague nature marketing.
topics.sourceEstablishes: IUCN guidance provides evidence-informed principles and implementation considerations for rewilding.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: The label ‘rewilding’ does not itself prove ecological recovery or determine the right intervention for a place.
topics.atlasContextNote: The map shows context; project outcomes require their own evidence.

topics.name: Climate Solutions
topics.title: Climate Solutions — Mitigation, Adaptation and Evidence | 4PLANET
topics.description: Explore climate solutions across energy, land, cities and human systems with IPCC evidence and clear separation between proposed action, delivery and measured outcome.
topics.answer: Climate solutions include actions that reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, remove carbon, reduce exposure and vulnerability, or strengthen resilience. Their value depends on context, scale, trade-offs, implementation and evidence.
keyFacts: Mitigation and adaptation solve different parts of the climate problem.
A solution category is not proof of a successful project.
Costs, co-benefits and trade-offs vary by place and system.
topics.happening: 4PLANET connects solution categories to energy, land, company and place context rather than publishing a single ranked list.
topics.whyItMatters: People searching for solutions need to know what can work, where it fits and what evidence would prove delivery and outcome.
topics.sourceEstablishes: IPCC AR6 synthesizes assessed mitigation and adaptation options, their feasibility and system context.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: An assessed option does not guarantee success for a specific project, company or location.
topics.atlasContextNote: ATLAS context is evidence input, not a ranking of solutions.

sources.label: AR6 Working Group III — Mitigation of Climate Change

topics.name: Environmental Jobs
topics.title: Environmental Jobs — Green Work and Ways to Help | 4PLANET
topics.description: Understand green jobs and practical routes into environmental work, connected to organisations, missions and ways to contribute through 4PLANET.
topics.answer: Green jobs are decent jobs that contribute to preserving or restoring the environment, either through the goods and services produced or through more environmentally sustainable production processes.
keyFacts: Environmental work exists in established and emerging sectors.
Job title alone does not determine environmental value.
Skills, location and actual employer activity matter.
topics.happening: 4PLANET connects this topic to its actor and participation layers so discovery can lead toward real organisations and roles rather than a static article.
topics.whyItMatters: Many people want to help but do not know where their existing skills fit. Search discovery can become a path into meaningful work and contribution.
topics.sourceEstablishes: The ILO defines green jobs and describes how work can contribute through environmental goods, services or improved production processes.
topics.sourceDoesNotEstablish: A role advertised as ‘green’ is not automatically high-impact, legitimate or a good fit for a particular person.
topics.atlasContextNote: The map provides system context; jobs and organisations require their own records.
